strengths: Proposes a simple and useful inference-time framework, BACO, for combining a base model and its aligned counterpart via token-level routing to navigate the diversity-quality trade-off without fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three open-ended generation settings, many lexical and semantic diversity metrics, two quality proxies, multiple routing variants, several baseline categories, and an additional OLMo model-family check.

The paper goes beyond short-form automatic metrics by including discourse-level narrative diversity and a human evaluation of quality, diversity, and creativity, which is important for this problem domain.

The routing analysis is informative: random routing, probability/entropy routers, content-based routers, combined routers, base-aligned vs aligned-aligned collaboration, contribution patterns, and early stopping failure modes are all examined.

Presentation is generally clear, with a coherent motivation around alignment-induced diversity loss and a helpful distinction between Coverage and Dominance for controllability and Pareto-frontier contribution.
weaknesses: The central 21.3%/joint improvement claim relies heavily on custom aggregate Coverage/Dominance metrics whose normalization choices are consequential. The feasible region is anchored to base/aligned default-temperature points and points outside it are discarded, which may materially shape conclusions; the paper does not provide enough sensitivity analysis for these choices.

Quality evidence is not fully convincing. Automatic quality mainly uses reward models and aligned-model perplexity, both imperfect proxies for human preference and potentially brittle under increased diversity. The human study is small, uses only 20 prompts per dataset and four LLM-aware annotators, and excludes the long-form setting.

The efficiency claims are under-supported. BACO requires coordinating two models at token level, and the paper discusses caching/speculative decoding only as future or potential optimizations rather than reporting actual latency, memory, throughput, or cost relative to baselines that require multiple generations.

Implementation details are still somewhat ambiguous despite appendices. The formal mixture equation with binary routing does not fully clarify whether routing is based on sampled tokens, top tokens, or distributions in each variant, and the word-boundary/tokenization handling could affect reproducibility and output quality.

Baselines are reasonable but not exhaustive for the breadth of claims. Some relevant inference-time diversity/control methods are discussed but not empirically compared, and training-time diversity methods are excluded even though the paper sometimes frames results as state-of-the-art for optimizing diversity and quality broadly.

The human evaluation has possible biasing choices: automatic quality is used to match configurations, prompts are stratified toward shorter outputs, annotators are told not to penalize truncation in long responses, and agreement for diversity judgments is only fair to moderate.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the first page contains placeholders for code/data/reading list, and the reproducibility statement says code and scripts will be released upon publication rather than providing them for review.

The ethics statement says the work does not involve human subjects, but the paper reports human annotators and consent details. This inconsistency should be corrected, and the risks of diversity increasing harmful or unsafe outputs deserve more concrete evaluation rather than only a deployment caveat.

There are presentation and polish issues, including several grammatical errors, placeholder text, and occasional unclear terminology, which do not block understanding but reduce confidence in manuscript readiness.

strengths: The paper tackles a real and timely problem: alignment often narrows output diversity, and the idea of exploiting complementary base/aligned checkpoints at inference time is practically relevant for open-ended generation.

BACO is simple and reasonably well motivated. The router family gives a concrete design space, and the paper evaluates across instruction following, dialogue, and long-form narrative generation rather than only toy prompts.

The authors include multiple diversity metrics, compare against several inference-time baselines, add an aligned-aligned ablation, and discuss an observed failure mode where aggressive base routing can cause premature stopping.
The writing is generally clear, with useful qualitative examples and an explicit ethics statement acknowledging that diversity-enhancing methods may increase harmful generations without safeguards.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not fully supported by the evaluation design. The headline improvements depend on aggregated Coverage/Dominance metrics whose normalization is anchored to default base/aligned points and discards points outside the chosen feasible region. This can materially affect conclusions and makes it difficult to interpret whether BACO truly dominates standard sampling or whether the metric construction favors it.

The paper repeatedly claims single-pass and efficient inference, but the main routers require consulting both base and aligned models at token level, often including logits or sampled tokens from both. No wall-clock, FLOP, memory, or throughput results are provided, so the efficiency claims are largely unsupported.

The quality evaluation is weak for the strength of the claims. Perplexity under the aligned model is not an independent quality metric and can penalize valid diverse continuations; the reward model may also favor aligned-model style. The human study is small, limited to 20 prompts per dataset with 4 CS-background annotators, excludes the long-form setting, and reports low agreement for diversity judgments, yet is used to make broad claims about quality, diversity, and creativity.

Model and method selection appear vulnerable to cherry-picking. The paper reports “BACO best” and in the appendix reports “BACO All” as best Coverage across routers and summed Dominance across routers, which is not directly comparable to single baseline methods. It is unclear how router thresholds, temperature grids, and best variants were selected without test-set tuning.

Baselines are not sufficiently controlled. Some baselines have only Dominance and no Coverage, compute budgets are not matched, and several natural alternatives or stronger adaptations are missing or underdeveloped, such as fixed mixture decoding, contrastive-style decoding, compute-matched multi-sampling/reranking, and more careful prompt/paraphrase baselines.

The formal method description is imprecise. Equation (1) defines token-dependent binary weights over candidate tokens, which may not form a normalized probability distribution if interpreted literally, while the appendix describes routing decisions based on sampled/top tokens. This gap between formulation and implementation weakens soundness and reproducibility.

Reproducibility is inadequate for an ICML main-track paper making extensive empirical claims. The manuscript has blank Code/Data fields, does not provide exact automatic-evaluation prompt counts or all subset construction details, and omits enough implementation detail about grids, seeds, model-serving behavior, and metric model versions to make faithful reproduction difficult.

The contribution is useful but not highly original: it is an incremental extension of token-level collaborative decoding/guided decoding ideas such as NUDGING and CITER, with hand-crafted routing heuristics repurposed for diversity-quality trade-offs. The new framing is interesting, but the evidence does not yet establish a robust new state of the art.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: alignment improves quality but reduces output diversity in open-ended generation. The proposed BACO framework is simple, intuitive, and practically attractive because it uses an available base/aligned model pair at inference time without retraining.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The authors test instruction following, dialogue, and long-form creative writing; compare against single-model temperature sweeps, prompting, decoding, ensemble, and NUDGING-style baselines; and report both lexical and semantic diversity-quality tradeoffs.

The routing analysis is useful. The paper does not just present one router, but studies random, probability/entropy, punctuation/function-word, combined, judge-based, and aligned-aligned variants. The ablations support the claim that base-aligned collaboration and carefully chosen routing matter.

The paper includes human evaluation for quality, diversity, and creativity, and the results are directionally consistent with the automatic evaluation. The qualitative examples also make the intended behavior of the method easy to understand.

Presentation is generally clear, and the paper provides substantial appendix detail on metrics, routing rules, datasets, human annotation instructions, and reproducibility plans. The ethics section acknowledges that increasing diversity may also increase harmful-generation risk.
weaknesses: The central empirical evidence relies heavily on automatic diversity and reward-model quality proxies. These are reasonable for scale, but the paper’s strong claims about improved quality-diversity tradeoffs would be more convincing with deeper calibration of the reward model, robustness to alternative reward models, or more extensive human evaluation.

The aggregate Coverage and Dominance metrics are somewhat custom and can obscure important behavior. In particular, points outside the base/aligned reference region are discarded, and several baseline categories report limited aggregate information, making it harder to judge whether the comparison fully captures their best achievable tradeoff.

The method’s efficiency claims are under-evaluated. BACO requires running or at least consulting two models during token-level decoding, yet the paper mostly argues efficiency qualitatively via sparsity/caching/speculative decoding rather than reporting wall-clock latency, memory overhead, or throughput against baselines.

The human study is helpful but small: 20 prompts per dataset, 3 outputs per method, and four CS-background annotators. It also excludes the long-form setting and samples shorter prompts to reduce annotator burden, so the human evidence does not fully validate the broader claims.

The method has a clear failure mode: aggressive routing to the base model can cause premature stopping or incomplete generations. The paper discusses this honestly, but the proposed restart workaround is not quantitatively evaluated and could affect both cost and quality.

Originality is solid but not exceptional. The main contribution is a clean application of token-level model collaboration to the diversity-quality tradeoff, combining existing ideas from base/aligned model agreement, routing heuristics, and multiobjective evaluation rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete at submission time. The paper promises code/configuration/evaluation scripts upon publication, but exact implementation choices for serving, threshold sweeps, baseline tuning, and some evaluation components would need the released code to be reliably reproduced.
